questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Votes held by a federal member
questions.learningObjective: Explain how federal vote shares are determined
questions.stem: Item 0001: a federal member holds 12 of 100 council votes; what does that imply for its influence?

options.text: A member's vote share reflects its population and negotiated federal weight.
A member's votes equal its share of national land area.
options.misconception: confuses population weight with land area

options.text: A member with the capital gets every federal vote.
options.misconception: treats capital location as vote monopoly

options.text: Votes are split equally among all members regardless of size.
options.misconception: assumes equal representation in a federal council

questions.explanation: Federal vote shares usually track population and negotiated weights, not land area or capital status. Equal splitting would ignore size differences among members.
questions.hint: Think about population and negotiated weights.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a federal centre sits in one member
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a federal capital sits in one member
questions.stem: Item 0002: a table shows the federal centre in one member despite a geographic midpoint elsewhere; what explains it?

options.text: It must sit at the exact geographic centre of the country.
options.misconception: confuses political centre with geographic midpoint

options.text: The centre sits in one member because of a political compromise among members.
It sits in the largest member by population.
options.misconception: assumes capital follows population size

options.text: It moves each term to a different member.
options.misconception: treats capital as rotating office

questions.explanation: Capital placement is usually a political compromise, not a geographic midpoint or population contest. Rotating capitals are rare and not the default.
questions.hint: Focus on political compromise among members.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A devolution of powers downward
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of devolving powers downward
questions.stem: Item 0003: powers move downward to regions; what is the main trade-off?

answer.exemplar: Devolution lets local needs shape policy, but it can create uneven standards and coordination costs across regions; national goals may be harder to enforce.

questions.explanation: Devolution brings decisions closer to local needs, yet it risks uneven standards and higher coordination costs. National consistency can weaken.
questions.hint: Balance local fit against national consistency.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A minority overall and a majority in a district
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a minority overall can win a district majority
questions.stem: Item 0004: a party wins 45 percent of votes but 60 percent of seats in one district; compute the overrepresentation ratio.
questions.explanation: Divide seat share by vote share, 0.60 divided by 0.45 equals about 1.33. This shows district boundaries can amplify a group's representation.
questions.hint: Divide seat share by vote share.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Effective rate of protection
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the effective rate of protection measures

stimulus.body: A transit board reviews a tariff schedule. The nominal tariff on the final good is 20 percent, while imported inputs face a 10 percent tariff.

questions.stem: Item 0005: given those tariffs, which statement about effective protection is correct?

options.text: It equals the nominal tariff on the final good.
options.misconception: confuses nominal tariff with effective protection

options.text: It ignores tariffs on imported inputs.
options.misconception: overlooks input tariffs in value added

options.text: It measures protection on value added, not just on output.
It is always zero for exported goods.
options.misconception: assumes export status nullifies protection

questions.explanation: Effective protection compares value added under protection to free-trade value added, so input tariffs matter. The nominal rate alone is not enough.
questions.hint: Compare value added, not just output.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A free trade zone beside a partner's concession
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a free trade zone works beside a partner's concession
questions.stem: Item 0006: a free trade zone sits beside a partner's concession; what is its main effect?

options.text: The zone taxes all imports at the partner's rate.
options.misconception: confuses free zone with common external tariff

options.text: The zone eliminates every rule of origin.
options.misconception: assumes duty-free means no origin rules

options.text: The zone forces firms to export all output.
options.misconception: confuses free zone with export-processing zone

options.text: The zone lets duty-free inputs enter beside a partner's concession.

questions.explanation: A free trade zone allows duty-free inputs in a defined area, while origin rules and other controls often remain. It does not force all output to be exported.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A free trade zone against a customs union
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a free trade zone from a customs union
questions.stem: Item 0007: how does a free trade zone differ from a customs union?

options.text: A customs union shares an external tariff; a free zone does not.
A free trade zone collects a common external tariff.
options.misconception: attributes customs-union feature to free zone

options.text: A customs union keeps internal tariffs among members.
options.misconception: reverses internal tariff rules

options.text: Both terms describe the same level of integration.
options.misconception: treats distinct blocs as identical

questions.explanation: A customs union removes internal tariffs and adopts a common external tariff; a free trade zone removes internal tariffs but lets members set their own external tariffs.
questions.hint: Check whether external tariffs are shared.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a member gives up in a currency union
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a member sacrifices in a currency union
questions.stem: Item 0008: a member joins a currency union; what does it give up?

options.text: It keeps full control of its interest rates.
options.misconception: assumes currency union preserves monetary autonomy

options.text: It can devalue its currency to boost exports.
options.misconception: ignores loss of national currency

options.text: It only gives up fiscal policy, not monetary policy.
options.misconception: confuses fiscal and monetary sovereignty

options.text: It gives up independent monetary policy and exchange-rate adjustment.

questions.explanation: Sharing a currency removes independent monetary policy and exchange-rate devaluation. Fiscal policy may remain, but monetary tools are pooled.

answer.exemplar: The member has a measurable but not dominant share of council votes, so it can influence outcomes when coalitions form but cannot decide alone.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A devolution of powers downward
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of devolving powers downward

stimulus.body: A transit board moves transport planning to regional councils. National standards still set safety floors, while regions choose routes and fares.

questions.stem: Item 0011: what does this arrangement illustrate?

options.text: Devolution removes all national authority over the issue.
options.misconception: equates devolution with full independence

options.text: Devolution guarantees identical rules in every region.
options.misconception: confuses decentralization with uniformity

options.text: Devolution always lowers total public spending.
options.misconception: assumes local control cuts costs automatically

options.text: Powers move down to let local needs shape policy.

questions.explanation: Regions gain route and fare choices while national safety floors remain, showing devolution rather than full independence or uniformity.

questions.topic: A minority overall and a majority in a district
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a minority overall can win a district majority
questions.stem: Item 0012: a party wins 40 percent of votes but 55 percent of seats in one district; what explains it?

options.text: District lines pack one group, creating a majority in that district.
The group must be a national majority to win the district.
options.misconception: confuses district majority with national majority

options.text: The result follows from random voter turnout alone.
options.misconception: attributes district outcome to turnout noise

options.text: The district has more voters than any other district.
options.misconception: equates district size with majority status

questions.explanation: Packed district lines can give a group a district majority even with a smaller national share. Turnout or district size alone does not explain it.
questions.hint: Think about how district lines pack voters.

questions.stem: Item 0021: a tariff is 25 percent on output and 10 percent on inputs; what does effective protection reflect?

answer.exemplar: Effective protection reflects the change in value added caused by both tariffs, so a high output tariff with lower input tariffs raises protection on value added.
